name: uv
summary: A Python package and project manager written in Rust that resolves, locks and installs dependencies, and installs Python itself, from one fast binary.
intro: uv is a single static binary with no Python dependency of its own. It covers jobs that used to need pip, pip-tools, pipx, Poetry, pyenv, twine and virtualenv: `uv add` writes a dependency into `pyproject.toml`, resolves it with `pubgrub-rs` (a Rust port of the PubGrub algorithm), records the answer in `uv.lock` and installs it into a `.venv` next to the project. `uv run` locks and syncs before running anything, so the environment is never out of date; in CI, `uv sync --locked` fails instead of updating a stale lockfile. `uv.lock` is universal: one TOML file covers every operating system, architecture and Python version, and `uv export` turns it into the standard `pylock.toml` for other installers. Around that sit `uvx` (run a command-line tool in a throwaway environment), `uv python install` (portable CPython builds from python-build-standalone, which Astral maintains), PEP 723 single-file scripts, Cargo-style workspaces and a `uv pip` interface that works as a drop-in for pip commands. A global cache with hardlinks or copy-on-write keeps repeated installs fast and small on disk.

uv is built by Astral, the company behind Ruff. In March 2026 Astral announced an agreement to join OpenAI as part of the Codex team; Charlie Marsh wrote that OpenAI will keep supporting the open-source tools, and the `astral-sh` GitHub organisation now describes its tools as “from @OpenAI”. uv is still versioned 0.x: minor releases carry breaking changes, as 0.13.0 (October 2026) did by making Python 3.15 the default download.
strengths: Fast: in Astral’s launch benchmark it was 8 to 10 times faster than pip and pip-tools without a cache and 80 to 115 times faster with a warm one
One tool from Python install to lockfile to running tools, with no Python needed to install it
A universal lockfile, so a Mac laptop and a Linux CI runner install from the same `uv.lock`
Follows the packaging standards: `[project]` metadata, PEP 735 dependency groups, PEP 723 scripts and `pylock.toml` export
limits: `uv.lock` is uv’s own format; other tools need an export, and some uv features can’t be expressed in `pylock.toml`
Pre-1.0 versioning: a minor version bump can break builds, so pin the uv version in CI
One company sets the roadmap, and that company agreed in March 2026 to join OpenAI; OpenAI has said it will keep supporting the open-source tools
Universal resolution is stricter than resolving for one machine: every dependency must work across the project’s whole `requires-python` range

snippet.title: A project, a lockfile, a one-off tool and a standard export (uv 0.13.0)
source: uv init --bare app && cd app      # just a pyproject.toml
uv add httpx                      # resolve, write uv.lock, create .venv, install
uvx ruff --version                # a tool in a cached, throwaway environment: ruff 0.17.0
uv export -o pylock.toml          # the PEP 751 lockfile, for installers other than uv
uv sync --locked                  # in CI: install exactly what uv.lock says, or fail

story: By the early 2020s a Python project could need half a dozen tools: pyenv for the interpreter, virtualenv for environments, pip to install, pip-tools to lock, pipx for command-line tools, Poetry or PDM to manage the project. Astral, the company Charlie Marsh founded in 2023 around the Ruff linter, set out to build “a Cargo for Python” instead.

uv shipped in February 2024 as a deliberately narrow first step: a Rust drop-in for `pip`, `pip-tools` and `virtualenv` that existing projects could adopt with no configuration. Astral took over Armin Ronacher’s experimental Rye project at the same time, folding its ideas in. In August 2024 uv grew into the full tool: `uv lock`, `uv sync` and `uv run` with cross-platform lockfiles, `uv tool` and `uvx`, `uv python install` and PEP 723 scripts. Astral adopted python-build-standalone, the portable CPython builds uv installs, from Gregory Szorc in December 2024.

By August 2025 Astral counted over 100 million installs a month across its tools and 500 million requests a day to uv, and launched pyx, a hosted package registry designed as a backend for uv. In March 2026 Astral agreed to join OpenAI’s Codex team, promising to keep building the tools in the open.

choices.choice: Start as a drop-in for pip and pip-tools
choices.why: Copying an interface people already used made adoption nearly free, and solving installation first gave the later, more opinionated project commands a solid base.

choices.choice: A single static binary with no Python dependency
choices.why: uv can be installed before any Python exists and then install Python itself, avoiding the `pip` versus `pip3` versus `pip3.7` confusion of tools that live inside an interpreter.
The first release locked for one platform, like pip-tools. Since August 2024 `uv.lock` records the packages for every OS, architecture and Python version, so teams on mixed machines share one file.

choices.choice: A global cache linked into environments
choices.why: Hardlinks and copy-on-write let many virtual environments share one copy of each package, so recreating an environment avoids downloading or building anything again and uses little extra disk.

timeline.text: uv released in February as a pip and pip-tools replacement; Astral takes over Rye
August: project management, cross-platform lockfiles, tools and Python installs
pyx, Astral’s package registry for uv, enters beta
March: Astral agrees to join OpenAI’s Codex team
June: `uv audit` and opt-in malware checks in preview
October: uv 0.13.0 makes Python 3.15 the default
